lines.text: Why does space begin at exactly one hundred kilometres?
Partly, because it's a round number.
The original calculation gave an awkward figure, close to a hundred.
The air-sports federation's own account calls it, quote, the very round number of one hundred.
Then in 2018, a paper by Jonathan McDowell argued the line is close to eighty kilometres, not a hundred.
The United States had given astronaut wings above fifty miles, which is also about eighty.
In 1962, an X-15 pilot reached ninety-five kilometres. Over one line, under the other.
So which pilots actually went to space? That's level seven, and the full video is linked right here.
